events.description: Al-Annabi named overall emir of AQIM after Droukdel's death.
Abdelmalek Droukdel killed in French-led counterterrorism operation.
GSPC formally merged into al-Qaeda to become AQIM (2006-2007), overseen by Droukdel; Younis al-Mauritani helped negotiate.
Abu Muhammad al-Masri assassinated in Iran by Israelis with CIA/Trump administration help.
After bin Laden's death, al-Annabi renewed AQIM's allegiance (bay'ah) to Zawahiri.
US Treasury designation revealed head of al-Qaeda's military committee based in Iran.
US and Afghan forces got Asim Umar's courier to Zawahiri.
Biden speech on over-the-horizon operations in case al-Qaeda returns to Afghanistan.
UN Monitoring Team report on Afghanistan: Taliban-al-Qaeda aligned, presence in 15 provinces, Jabhat al-Nasr wing, footnote on Sirajuddin Haqqani and Hattin Shura.
Jalaluddin Haqqani helped bin Laden escape Tora Bora in late 2001, per bin Laden's bodyguard.
Anas Haqqani attended Taliban-US negotiations in Doha.
9/11 Commission report published with last US government al-Qaeda wire diagram.
The US drone campaign against al-Qaeda leaders in Pakistan took off in 2008 at the end of Bush's term and was handed to Obama.
Al-Qaeda established AQIS as a new branch.
Senior al-Qaeda figures including Saif al-Adel, Abu Muhammad al-Masri and Abu al-Khayr al-Masri were freed from Iranian detention. Joscelyn infers the Hittin Shura was stood up around then.
Biden spoke of building over-the-horizon capabilities to strike al-Qaeda 'if they return to Afghanistan'.

key_claims: The Hittin Shura is al-Qaeda's central decision-making body, probably stood up around 2015 and likely numbering in the dozens, but its membership and function have never been publicly explained.
Releases of legacy al-Qaeda veterans from Iranian detention in 2015, along with the rise of ISIS, probably drove al-Qaeda's internal reorganization.
The UN calls Sirajuddin Haqqani part of the wider al-Qaeda leadership, yet he is not on the Hittin Shura, so his place in the structure is unclear.
Al-Qaeda is already in Afghanistan rather than 'returning', and has fought alongside the Taliban throughout.
The UN estimates 8,000-10,000 foreign fighters in Afghanistan, many tied to al-Qaeda, and al-Qaeda helps recruit and organize them into groups.
The Haqqani Network is so entangled with al-Qaeda that the line between the two cannot be drawn, and al-Qaeda leaders have been killed in non-Haqqani areas such as Helmand and Nimruz.
Over-the-horizon counterterrorism from Pakistan, Iran, or Central Asia is unlikely, so basing and target discrimination among foreign fighters are major problems.
US claims that two-thirds or three-quarters of al-Qaeda's leadership was killed or captured were meaningless, because the total pool was never known.
